extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in mathematics or computer science studying discrete math and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and standard proof techniques for functions: composition, restriction, identity, one-to-one (injective), onto (surjective), inverses, and related equivalences; includes worked examples and exercises for practicing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of function (existence and uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation f ⊆ A × B is a function from A to B iff for every a ∈ A there exists a unique b ∈ B with (a,b) ∈ f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that a relation is a function should show existence and uniqueness for each a ∈ A; when showing a relation fails to be a function, give a counterexample: either an a with no paired b, or an a with two different b's. (Example and explanation appear in the text surrounding the proof that g◦f is a function.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C then g ◦ f : A → C and (g ◦ f)(x) = g(f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving composition is a function, exhibit for arbitrary a ∈ A the element b = f(a) and then c = g(b) to show existence, and argue uniqueness. Note: composition of relations specialized to functions yields the convenient formula (g ◦ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Composition of functions is associative (use Theorem 4.2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of a function
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f : A → B and C ⊆ A, the restriction f↾C (notated f (cid:3) C in the text) is f ∩ (C × B); f↾C is a function from C to B and for all c ∈ C, f(c) = (f↾C)(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove f↾C is a function follow the same existence/uniqueness pattern restricted to C. Also: g = f↾C iff g ⊆ f (exercise). Use this to reason about equality and inclusion of restricted functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function properties (i_A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity i_A on A is the relation i_A(a) = a for all a ∈ A; i_A is both a function A → A and an equivalence relation on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i_A is one-to-one and onto. Use i_A in compositions to test inverses: for a bijection f, f^{-1} ◦ f = i_A and f ◦ f^{-1} = i_B. To prove equality of functions, often show pointwise equality (∀a, (g◦f)(a) = i_A(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: one-to-one (injective)
rubrics_metrics.description: f : A → B is one-to-one if ¬∃a1 ∈ A∃a2 ∈ A( f(a1) = f(a2) ∧ a1 ≠ a2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends reexpressing the negative definition as the positive equivalent (Theorem 5.2.3): f is one-to-one iff ∀a1 ∈ A ∀a2 ∈ A( f(a1) = f(a2) → a1 = a2). Typical proof strategy: assume f(a1) = f(a2) for arbitrary a1,a2 and derive a1 = a2. To show non-injectivity, give two distinct domain elements with same image (counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: onto (surjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: f : A → B is onto if ∀b ∈ B ∃a ∈ A( f(a) = b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (Theorem 5.2.3): f is onto iff Ran(f) = B. Typical proof strategy: let b be an arbitrary element of B and produce an a with f(a) = b. To show not onto, find a particular b ∈ B such that no a satisfies f(a) = b (i.e., ∃b ∈ B ∀a ∈ A f(a) ≠ b). The worked example (solving 2a/(a+1) = x) shows how attempting to construct a preimage can reveal problematic x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence forms for injective and surjective (Theorem 5.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. f is one-to-one iff ∀a1 ∈ A ∀a2 ∈ A( f(a1) = f(a2) → a1 = a2). 2. f is onto iff Ran(f) = B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logical manipulations (reexpressing negations) to convert negative definitions into positive forms that are easier to use in proofs. The theorem is used repeatedly as a proof template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity (Theorem 5.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C then (1) if f and g are one-to-one, so is g ◦ f; (2) if f and g are onto, so is g ◦ f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof pattern for injectivity: assume (g◦f)(a1) = (g◦f)(a2) → g(f(a1)) = g(f(a2)), use injectivity of g to get f(a1)=f(a2), then injectivity of f to get a1=a2. For surjectivity: let c ∈ C arbitrary; pick b with g(b)=c (g onto), then pick a with f(a)=b (f onto); then (g◦f)(a)=c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijection and one-to-one correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: A function that is both one-to-one and onto is called a one-to-one correspondence or bijection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bijections are important because they show sets have the same cardinality; for finite sets a bijection implies equal sizes. Many proofs and constructions rely on showing a function is a bijection via the standard injective/surjective strategies or by constructing explicit inverse functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse of a function: sufficient condition (Theorem 5.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B is one-to-one and onto, then f^{-1} : B → A (i.e., the inverse relation is a function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits into two parts for each b ∈ B: existence (use surjectivity to find an a with f(a)=b) and uniqueness (use injectivity to show that a is unique). This proof pattern (existence + uniqueness) is the standard way to prove ∃! statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of f^{-1} when it is a function
rubrics_metrics.description: If f^{-1} : B → A then for each b ∈ B, f^{-1}(b) = the unique a ∈ A such that f(a) = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a practical way to compute inverses: solve f(a) = b for a in terms of b. The textbook demonstrates solving an algebraic equation for a (e.g., solving 2a/(a+1)=x) to find preimages and identify values missing from the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse implies identity compositions (Theorem 5.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and f^{-1} is a function B → A, then f^{-1} ◦ f = i_A and f ◦ f^{-1} = i_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is pointwise: for arbitrary a ∈ A let b = f(a) and show f^{-1}(f(a)) = a. Use this identity form to reason about 'undoing' effects of functions and in uniqueness proofs of inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left and right inverses imply injectivity/surjectivity (Theorem 5.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. If there exists g : B → A with g ◦ f = i_A then f is one-to-one. 2. If there exists g : B → A with f ◦ g = i_B then f is onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea for injectivity: apply g to the equality f(a1)=f(a2) to obtain a1=a2. For surjectivity use the existence of g to produce preimages for arbitrary b ∈ B. Interpret existential statements by imagining a chosen g and then proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of bijection, inverse-as-function, and two-sided inverse (Theorem 5.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B the following are equivalent: (1) f is one-to-one and onto; (2) f^{-1} : B → A; (3) there exists g : B → A such that g ◦ f = i_A and f ◦ g = i_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove the circle of implications 1→2→3→1. This equivalence is central: existence of a two-sided inverse characterizes bijections. Use earlier theorems to chain implications rather than reproving facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of inverse (Theorem 5.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → A satisfy g ◦ f = i_A and f ◦ g = i_B then g = f^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use previously proven identities and composition associativity to show g equals the inverse relation; the text gives a short derivation using f^{-1}◦f = i_A and substitution. More direct elementwise proofs are possible (exercise mentioned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof templates guided by logical form (commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose proof structure matching the logical quantifiers: to prove ∀x∃y P(x,y) let x be arbitrary then construct y; to prove ∃!y P(x,y) prove existence and uniqueness separately; to prove equality of functions show pointwise equality ∀x f(x)=g(x) (use Theorem 5.1.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly emphasizes matching the proof strategy to quantifier structure (examples: proving onto, proving f^{-1} is a function, proving compositions equal the identity). It also suggests converting negative statements to equivalent positive forms to simplify proofs (e.g., injective definition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance of injectivity/onto under restriction and unions (exercises guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts used in exercises: (a) If f is one-to-one then f↾C is one-to-one. (b) If f↾C is onto then f is onto. (c) If f and g are one-to-one and domains are disjoint, f ∪ g is one-to-one iff ranges are disjoint. (exercise statements describe these patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard closure/inheritance properties: prove by applying definitions on restricted domain or union and using previously established equivalences about injective/surjective. The exercises indicate typical techniques to test understanding.
